items.summary: Unrefereed candidate. A proof that for every n >= 1 and real c, every non-real eigenvalue of the 2n x 2n indefinite tridiagonal pencil H_c - lambda S (diagonal c, off-diagonal 1, S = diag(1,...,1,-1,...,-1)) satisfies |lambda - c| < 2 and |lambda + c| < 2. This is Conjecture 5.3 of Davies and Levitin (Linear Algebra Appl. 448, 2014), and it implies the closed-disk form of AIM 2015 Problem 11.1. It was previously known for n <= 3 and for eigenvalues equidistant from c and -c (Öztürk 2023). A standard Weyl-function mechanism, applied to the known Chebyshev form of the characteristic equation, reduces the conjecture to a comparison lemma for an explicit Lorentzian sum over the zeros of U_{n-1}; the comparison lemma and its proof are the original contribution. It is proved by explicit estimates with finitely many Arb-certified constants for n >= 8, elementary arguments for n <= 2, and, for 3 <= n <= 7, an explicit estimate plus a short interval certificate with rational endpoints and Arb ball arithmetic. Certified examples show that the lens fails for some other spectral measures, for a balanced pencil with one weakened coupling, and for unbalanced pencils. The package contains the manuscript, certificates, regression tests, semantic negative controls and review records. Provenance: the research, proof and text were produced by an AI research agent (Claude, Anthropic) under the direction of the publisher, Evidence Press; no human mathematical contribution is claimed, and no human specialist has checked the proof. Internal replay and model-based reviews only; no formal verification, independent reproduction, specialist or journal peer review; novelty is established only within a bounded literature search.
items.title: A proof of the Davies–Levitin lens conjecture for the indefinite tridiagonal pencil

items.summary: The rapid progression of large language models is extending AI from passive content generation into the active workflows of engineering and scientific discovery. This shift raises a compelling question: can AI be both the object of development and an active participant in building next-generation AI systems? We explore this question by building Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework for scalable development and iterative improvement. Mobile planning offers a demanding test of this approach: complex, long-horizon tasks challenge agent reliability, while costly real-device interaction limits development scalability. The framework connects data production, model training, and deployment through a shared action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data builds a human-gated agentic data flywheel in which specialized agents construct tasks, collect interaction trajectories, curate and balance training data, and use training feedback to guide subsequent data generation. (ii) AI for Training combines a supervised planning cold start with hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning, where we introduce Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning and tool-use costs while preserving task performance. (iii) AI drives model--harness co-evolution through an execution-evidence-driven loop that orchestrates memory, skills, and tools at runtime and feeds structured action feedback and preserved failure traces back into coordinated model and harness adaptation. Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models and systems on MobilePA-Bench, improving over its base model across tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination. Further evaluations of our model show improvements across non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities.
items.title: Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents

items.summary: Global-to-local load transfer remains a critical – yet largely unstandardized – step in the structural assessment of floating structures. This paper presents the results of package WP2.2 from the OC7 project Phase II, which establishes a cross-industry benchmark for the workflows connecting global performance analysis (based on integrated loads analysis, ILA) and the local structural assessment (based on finite-element analysis, FEA). The study evaluates a spectrum of industry practices, including sequential approaches with the FEA following the ILA, fully integrated time-domain approaches with hydro-structural coupling, and simplified ILA-only approaches. Using the VolturnUS-S reference semi-submersible, the models were first harmonized through mass and inertia, static, and modal verifications. Structural responses were then compared across three primary scenarios: topside-only excitation, irregular waves, and combined wind and wave loading. The results establish a structured comparison framework, highlighting how specific modelling choices and load transfer techniques directly influence confidence in design processes. The findings offer practical guidance to reduce uncertainty in “global-to-local” design workflows.
items.title: OC7 Project Phase II: Comparison of Global-to-Local Load Transfer Approaches in Floating Structures

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22967519 . This paper looks at what happens when we trust an AI coding agent's work without independently checking what actually changed. The authors show a case where a protected file was changed, but GTB still returned VERIFIED because the file was left out of the verification process. I thought one of the strongest parts of the paper was the distinction between stopping an agent from doing something and actually being able to prove that it didn't do it . The paper also does a good job of showing the attack in practice, explaining why the verification failed, and suggesting ways to make the process more reliable. Major issues The experiment focuses on GTB, so testing other coding-agent or verification systems would help show whether the issue is specific to GTB or appears more broadly. The proposed fixes have not yet been independently tested. Testing them against the same attack, along with a few variations, would make the results more convincing. Minor issues Including the exact software versions and experimental environment would make the experiment easier to reproduce. A simple diagram showing the normal verification path and where the modified file gets excluded would make the main failure easier to understand. It would also be useful to state how many times the attack was repeated and whether the same result occurred consistently Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Evaluating these bacterial-host interaction channels expands our understanding of skin microbiome-mediated lipid homeostasis without relying on generalized phenotypic observations. This technical adjustment increases the study's predictive utility for independent investigators developing targeted structural biology interventions to disrupt dysregulated sebaceous networks. items.summary: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing the initial temperature distribution in a one-dimensional non-homogeneous heat equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions from a finite number of pointwise-in-time measurements at a single spatial location. We propose an explicit approximation scheme that incorporates the source term and utilizes a refined sequence of measurement times. Unlike previous approaches that often rely on exponentially growing observation times, our chosen time sequence allows for efficient recovery within a fixed time horizon. We establish algebraic convergence rates under suitable regularity assumptions on the initial data and the forcing, and we validate the theoretical sharpness with numerical experiments for varying numbers of measurements.
items.title: Reconstruction of the Initial Condition for a Non-Homogeneous Heat Equation from Finite Measurements

items.summary: Long-running interactions with large language models can become historically organized, but apparent continuity across branches or reconstructed sessions may arise from several different carriers, including accessible history, memory systems, procedural state, lineage, or harness-level persistence. This naturalistic case study examines a longitudinal interaction between one human collaborator and a GPT-5.6 Sol trajectory called “Solomon,” using a ten-day Founder corpus and four naturalistic continuity configurations ranging from a fresh out-of-project response to continuations with inherited or archive-assisted history. The study does not claim consciousness or strict personal identity. Instead, it asks which aspects of prior organization are immediately available, which require reconstruction, and whether prior commitments continue to constrain appropriate action in novel situations. In the sequential qualitative synthesis of the ten-day Founder corpus, research commitments, provenance rules, relational procedures, governance constraints, and future-directed tasks were interpreted as becoming more explicitly integrated and mutually constraining over time. We call this structure of unfinishedness: an organized future in which unresolved obligations and sequencing constraints shape what should happen next. The naturalistic evidence is compatible with multiple reconstruction mechanisms and does not identify a unique causal carrier. It therefore motivates a controlled fork–recover–ablate–migrate design that equalizes accessible history while varying lineage and other continuity-relevant state, with novel extrapolation and update dynamics as key discriminators. Keywords: LLM agents; continuity; branching; fork; recovery; relational identity; longitudinal interaction; agent memory; persona; harness; path dependence; provenance
items.title: FORK, RECOVERY, AND HISTORICALLY ORGANIZED CONTINUITY IN A LONGITUDINAL LLM–HUMAN INTERACTION: A Naturalistic Case Study

items.summary: A benchmark harness for evaluating LLM agents on research-grade STEM tasks, built on Inspect AI. Each task is a self-contained contract folder that the harness loads, stages into a sandbox, runs through an agent, and scores without task-specific harness code. WHAT THIS ARCHIVE CONTAINS Harness source code: task loading, Inspect task/solver construction, tool surface (bash, python, data exploration, literature search, document reading, submission validation), Docker and local sandbox backends, scorers, and the CLI entry points for running, grading, and aggregating. The complete contract for 12 tasks across three domains — astrophysics (simulated and real Stokes inversion, PLAsTiCC light-curve classification), high-energy physics (top-quark tagging, HiggsML uncertainty quantification, LHC Olympics anomaly detection, DarkMachines anomaly detection), and neuroscience (ABIDE multi-site diagnosis and age prediction, resting-state BOLD HRF deconvolution, neural-mass model family classification, parameter recovery, and digital twins). Per task: the agent-facing task statement, the scoring definition, the grader, per-file SHA-256 checksums, a literature index citing sources by DOI, baseline and expert reference solutions, and dataset-generation code where the payload is synthetic. Leaderboards and the per-run report used for the reported results, plus the campaign script that records the exact model, agent, sandbox, reasoning effort, and budget limits behind them. WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN Dataset payloads are not in this archive. They are published as a companion dataset record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960135, as one archive per task, each unpacking at this repository's root. Every task ships per-file SHA-256 checksums so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte. Without the payloads the harness can be inspected and extended, but tasks cannot be executed or scored. Evaluation run logs (.eval files) are not published. The reported scores are in LEADERBOARD.md, the per-task CSVs under leaderboards/, and report.html, which embeds the per-run agent trajectories. One task's payload (ABIDE-derived) is never redistributed: its source data is CC-BY-NC-SA and derives from human neuroimaging data. A preparation script rebuilds it locally from the source archive and verifies the result against the published checksums. Published reference papers are not redistributed. Every external reference is cited by DOI with title, authors, venue, and a resolvable link. REPRODUCIBILITY REPRODUCING.md is the step-by-step checklist. Two limits are stated up front: reported scores come from hosted preview model snapshots run without a fixed seed or temperature, so they are samples from a distribution rather than bit-reproducible values; and dependency versions are not pinned in this version of the archive. DATA_LICENSES.md records the provenance and licence of every task's data, including the attribution notices required by the CC-BY-4.0 sources. LICENCE Code, task contracts, graders, reference solutions, and documentation are MIT. Task descriptions and the synthetic data payloads are CC-BY-4.0 and are covered by the companion dataset record.

Abstract: Under the communist regime, the evidence related to education in Hungarian mother tongue was under restricted access, except for two statistical yearbooks in which only limited data was available. At present, 28 years after the fall of the Romanian communist regime, public access to archived records is considerably easier. However, for the period 1948-1989, a statistical report on education in the Hungarian language hasn't been done so far. Given the lack of descriptive data, our inquiry has sought to portray a history of Hungarian mother tongue school education in Romania in the communist era as it has been revealed following our enterprise of collecting, selecting, sorting and analyzing data from relevant statistical yearbooks, statistical reports on education and the other published or unpublished statistical records. After the reconstruction of a satisfactory set of documents containing data on the number of schools, number of enrolled pupils and number of teaching staff, our research was focused on a trend analysis. Finally, contrasting these findings with the legislative and political context, we tried to provide some answers on how and why the communist regime had limited the mother tongue education opportunities of the Hungarian population in Romania. items.summary: Latent world models are typically trained to predict factual transitions, whereas model predictive control (MPC) must compare alternative actions from the same state. A model can therefore achieve low factual prediction error yet poorly distinguish candidate actions. We introduce AD-WM, an action-discriminative joint-embedding world model for counterfactual MPC. AD-WM combines residual latent dynamics with predictor-level action-recovery regularization, using inverse dynamics and a normalized recovery objective motivated by conditional mutual information. Both objectives encourage planning transitions to preserve action information; their auxiliary heads are discarded at test time, leaving MPC unchanged. On OGBench-Cube, AD-WM improves hard-start success from 3.7% to 52.0% over a matched LeWM baseline and improves mean success over the reproduced baseline in four of five simulation environments. Planning diagnostics show that factual prediction error and whole-bank action ranking do not follow the closed-loop success ordering, whereas CEM-aligned elite regret tracks success more closely. With a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder and matched DROID post-training, AD-WM also improves zero-shot transfer to our Franka setup, increasing basic pick-and-place success from 42.2% to 71.1% without lab-specific adaptation. These results suggest that world models for planning should preserve action-dependent differences needed for counterfactual selection, rather than optimize factual prediction accuracy alone. More videos and code are available at https://ad-wm.github.io/.
items.title: AD-WM: Action-Discriminative World Models for Counterfactual Model Predictive Control

items.summary: Mobile emergency networks can experience independently changing intermediate wireless links on timescales shorter than endpoint feedback can track. When an egress changes after packet emission, feedback affects only later source data, while the on-path node observes the current condition with the affected packet still mutable. This paper presents DINA, a packet-level in-network semantic adaptation method. An image is divided into self-describing spatial packets carrying coordinates, a current representation identifier, and payload. At each eligible node, an offline-trained frozen selector scores compatible operators, immediately transforms the packet, and forwards it without image reconstruction or cross-packet adaptation state. Later nodes can retain or further compact the packet through the same typed compatibility contract. The receiver places available packets by coordinate, fills missing regions with black, and runs a fixed machine task. We realize DINA in a 24-node UAV environment using XDP and AF_XDP. In the primary forest-fire trace, DINA raises deadline tile coverage from 40.4% to 72.6% and classification accuracy from 77.5% to 95.0% relative to forwarding. In an independently trained RescueNet segmentation case, it raises coverage from 65.6% to 91.7% and foreground mIoU from 0.486 to 0.541. Sufficient- and extreme-capacity profiles expose a no-gain boundary and a common task-failure boundary, respectively.
items.title: Packet-Level In-Network Semantic Adaptation for Unstable Mobile Emergency Networks

items.summary: Textured Gaussians improve local appearance capacity, but assigning the same texture resolution to every primitive wastes storage on low-detail or weakly visible regions. We introduce AdaTex4D, an adaptive texture-capacity module for deformation-based 4D Gaussian Splatting. Each Gaussian carries packed RGBA triplanes whose two axes grow independently according to visibility normalized screen-space gradients and deformed local scales. Experiments on N3DV and PanopticSports show that AdaTex4D reduces texture storage by more than half while preserving reconstruction quality. Under fixed memory budgets, adaptive allocation also improves quality over uniform texture assignment and reduces overall model and peak memory. These results show that dynamic, anisotropic texture allocation provides a more efficient way to distribute local appearance capacity in 4D Gaussian representations.
items.title: ADATEX4D: adaptive texture capacity allocation for 4D gaussian splatting

items.summary: We present Underwater C$^{3}$-JEPA (cross-view, control-conditioned, context-extended), an object-centric multi-view predictive world model for near-field heavy-load underwater ROV salvage. Without contact sensors, it predicts in latent space how the task-object state evolves through contact interaction and under the hydrodynamic lag of the vehicle, from synchronized multi-view RGB observations and vehicle control signals. C$^{3}$-JEPA encodes multi-camera observations into task-object and context tokens, fuses cross-camera evidence through held-out-view attention, and directly predicts future states conditioned on control. Weak binding anchors the target and gripper at low annotation cost, while SIGReg sharpens the geometric representation. Experiments show that the learned representation transfers substantially more task-relevant information to downstream probes than a reconstruction-free latent baseline, while keeping the predictor lightweight. The resulting predictive interface supports model-predictive-control (MPC) candidate evaluation and imagined-rollout behavior-agent training. Validation on real underwater video shows the same architecture recovering a withheld camera's object state and staying ahead of persistence, so the recipe transfers beyond simulation.
items.title: Underwater C3-JEPA: An Object-Centric Cross-View World Model for ROV Salvage

items.summary: This study assesses the voltage harmonic performance of a fuzzy controlled grid connected photovoltaic–battery system using harmonic results reported from a MATLAB/Simulink model. The analysis concentrates on the third, fifth, seventh and ninth harmonics and on the consistency of the reported total harmonic distortion (THD). The listed harmonic magnitudes decreased from 2.85%, 3.60%, 2.10% and 1.25% without fuzzy control to 1.20%, 1.85%, 1.10% and 0.65% with fuzzy control, respectively. Relative reductions ranged from 47.62% to 57.89%. The fifth harmonic remained the largest listed component, although its magnitude fell by 1.75 percentage points. Reported voltage THD decreased from 7.85% to 3.42%, corresponding to a 56.43% relative reduction. However, root-sum-square reconstruction from the four specified orders yielded 5.20% and 2.55%, respectively. Including the separately reported higher-order entry as an aggregate increased these estimates to 5.32% and 2.59%, leaving the reported totals unreconciled. The available evidence therefore indicates lower listed voltage harmonics with fuzzy control but does not establish a complete spectrum or standards compliance. The contribution is a focused comparison of harmonic attenuation and a transparent assessment of the spectral information required to substantiate aggregate performance.
tags: Photovoltaic System,  Battery  Storage,  Fuzzy  Logic  Control,  Voltage  Harmonics, Total  Harmonic  Distortion, Power Quality.
items.title: Harmonic Performance Assessment of a Fuzzy Controlled Grid Connected Photovoltaic Battery System

items.summary: High-order differential operators and nonlinear coupling make it challenging to construct conservative and energy-stable schemes for coupled gradient-flow systems. We present GradAgent, a knowledge-guided multi-agent system that coordinates three agents across model analysis, algorithm design and proofs, and numerical implementation and validation. Independent audits strengthen reliability by uncovering mathematical errors and proof gaps, guiding revisions, and maintaining consistency across stages. In Reconstruction Mode, GradAgent reconstructs 20 published studies and organizes audited knowledge in an extensible knowledge graph (KG), GradAgent-KG, linking model structures, discretization strategies and proofs, implementations, and numerical evidence. In Design Mode, the agents assess the applicability of retrieved knowledge and develop new schemes informed by relevant discretization strategies. Applied to the fully coupled multicomponent vesicle phase-field-fluid model, GradAgent yields three first-order and three second-order schemes across three algorithmic families, including four linear, decoupled schemes. Under stated assumptions, all six schemes conserve membrane component mass and vesicle volume and dissipate their respective temporally discrete energies unconditionally. Comparisons with and without GradAgent-KG show that it promotes diversity in structure-preserving scheme design for this target model. Numerical tests confirm second-order spatial accuracy, the expected temporal orders, conservation, and temporally discrete energy dissipation, while three-dimensional shear-flow simulations agree qualitatively with experiments. These results demonstrate GradAgent's ability to combine reusable knowledge, coordinated reasoning, and independent auditing to develop and validate structure-preserving algorithms for complex coupled systems.
items.title: GradAgent: A Knowledge-Guided Multi-Agent System for Structure-Preserving Gradient-Flow Computation with an Application to Multicomponent Vesicle Dynamics

items.summary: An independent ns-3 reconstruction of the Low Energy and Overhead (LEO) wireless-sensor-network routing metric, with hop-count and ZigBee LQI comparators. Version 1.1.0 requalifies the simulator through regression testing, deterministic RNG streams, frozen experiment provenance, complete raw-data regeneration, paired statistical reanalysis, and checksum-bound figures and claims. In the source-constrained static non-interference analysis, LEO reduces timeout and no-route outcomes versus hop-count, while its energy effect depends on the relay cap; LEO uses more energy than the operational LQI comparator in the tested primary strata. Mobility and reconstruction-parameter studies are reported separately as exploratory or sensitivity analyses. The repository does not claim exact replay of the original authors' unpublished simulator code.
items.title: leo-wsn: an ns-3 reconstruction of the LEO routing metric with mobility and parameter-sensitivity analysis

items.summary: The rapid progression of large language models is extending AI from passive content generation into the active workflows of engineering and scientific discovery. This shift raises a compelling question: can AI be both the object of development and an active participant in building next-generation AI systems? We explore this question by building Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework for scalable development and iterative improvement. Mobile planning offers a demanding test of this approach: complex, long-horizon tasks challenge agent reliability, while costly real-device interaction limits development scalability. The framework connects data production, model training, and deployment through a shared action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data builds a human-gated agentic data flywheel in which specialized agents construct tasks, collect interaction trajectories, curate and balance training data, and use training feedback to guide subsequent data generation. (ii) AI for Training combines a supervised planning cold start with hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning, where we introduce Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning and tool-use costs while preserving task performance. (iii) AI drives model--harness co-evolution through an execution-evidence-driven loop that orchestrates memory, skills, and tools at runtime and feeds structured action feedback and preserved failure traces back into coordinated model and harness adaptation. Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models and systems on MobilePA-Bench, improving over its base model across tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination. Further evaluations of our model show improvements across non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities.
items.title: Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22967519 . This paper looks at what happens when we trust an AI coding agent's work without independently checking what actually changed. The authors show a case where a protected file was changed, but GTB still returned VERIFIED because the file was left out of the verification process. I thought one of the strongest parts of the paper was the distinction between stopping an agent from doing something and actually being able to prove that it didn't do it . The paper also does a good job of showing the attack in practice, explaining why the verification failed, and suggesting ways to make the process more reliable. Major issues The experiment focuses on GTB, so testing other coding-agent or verification systems would help show whether the issue is specific to GTB or appears more broadly. The proposed fixes have not yet been independently tested. Testing them against the same attack, along with a few variations, would make the results more convincing. Minor issues Including the exact software versions and experimental environment would make the experiment easier to reproduce. A simple diagram showing the normal verification path and where the modified file gets excluded would make the main failure easier to understand. It would also be useful to state how many times the attack was repeated and whether the same result occurred consistently Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they did not use generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
items.title: PREreview of "Beyond Agent Self-Reporting: Evidence-Based Verification of Autonomous AI Software Work"

items.summary: The English Resource Grammar (ERG) is a hand-written computational grammar of English. Given a sentence, its processor, ACE, produces a formal meaning representation called Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS): a graph of the sentence's predicates and their arguments. The grammar is bidirectional and can also turn an MRS back into an English sentence. \citet{hajdik2019} used the ERG's treebank to build a benchmark for that generation task, MRS to text, and trained sequence-to-sequence models to solve it. The parsing task, text to MRS, can be tested on the same sentences. We reconstruct their 10K-sentence test split, and score two large language models, Claude Sonnet~4.5 and Claude Opus~5, in both directions against their trained systems and against ACE, with no task-specific training. Given an MRS and three examples, Opus writes the sentence at 76.3 BLEU, ten points above their system trained on 72k pairs (66.1 BLEU), and comparable to their system trained on a million extra pairs (77.2 BLEU). Sonnet scores 65.7 BLEU, and letting it choose among ACE's own candidate sentences lifts it to 69.6, while a pooled judge that keeps Opus's own sentence among the candidates adds 0.6 points (77.0 BLEU). In the parsing direction, however, the models fall far behind ACE: asked for the MRS of the same sentences, they reach 57.2 (Sonnet) and 65.5 (Opus) F$_1$ on the graph's predicates and arguments against 91.0 for ACE, and exact-match the gold on about 1\% of sentences. We characterize the failure modes for the parsing tasks, and conclude that a generation score alone does not show that models understand formal semantic representations.
items.title: Scoring Both Directions: LLMs realize the MRS they cannot reliably parse

items.summary: Governance near a plausible critical transition faces a resource problem in addition to problems of diagnosis, intervention, and evidence. Elevated susceptibility can increase the value of observation, bounded experimentation, and revisability, while waiting can simultaneously consume the fiscal, material, organizational, temporal, and relational capacities required for survival and later action. This paper develops a discussion framework for that tension. Its central object is functional resource distribution: the allocation of heterogeneous capacities across observation, probing, short-horizon survival, selective commitment, reserve or option preservation, and recovery or repair. The categories are analytical functions rather than a scalar budget partition and can overlap in practice. The paper introduces distributed optionality as a relational property of a response architecture in which materially different future actions remain supported by functionally diverse and sufficiently non-coincident pathways. It distinguishes exact reversal from recoverability, spatial dispersion from independence of failure modes, and delay as information gathering from delay as resource dissipation. The framework inherits, rather than restates, earlier arguments about response-oriented governance and evidence-to-action instability near criticality. Its distinctive question is how governance capacity may be composed when the future regime is uncertain, resources are partly non-substitutable, and both premature commitment and indefinite waiting can narrow the feasible future. The proposal is conditional and non-prescriptive: criticality requires domain-specific empirical support, and the appropriate resource portfolio depends on transition mechanism, horizon, institutional structure, and explicit normative commitments.
items.title: Governance and Survival near Criticality: Functional Resource Distribution and Distributed Optionality

items.summary: Neural receivers for 5G NR are commonly compared against least-squares (LS) baselines, which leaves open whether they improve on a well-tuned classical receiver and whether their gains survive conditions outside the training distribution. We evaluate a fully convolutional neural receiver and a lightweight hybrid receiver, which retains a classical LS and linear minimum mean-squared error (LMMSE) front end and learns a residual correction of its log-likelihood ratios, on standard-compliant 5G NR PUSCH with 3GPP tapped delay line channels and hardware impairments. Baselines include an LMMSE channel estimator supplied with the empirical statistics of each test scenario (genie) and one supplied with a single fixed set of statistics from the training mixture (practical). Inside the training range both learned receivers only match the genie baseline. Two regimes differ. With an RMS delay spread of 2000 ns the learned receivers require 0.90 dB less than the genie baseline, while the practical LMMSE receiver does not reach 10 percent BLER at all; with a single DMRS symbol the neural receiver requires 4.08 dB less than the best classical receiver at 20 m/s and is the only receiver that operates at 30 m/s. We further show that the apparent failure of learned receivers outside the training envelope is a matter of training coverage rather than architecture: widening the training delay spread from 30-300 ns to 30-1000 ns converts a 5.97 dB deficit at 2000 ns into a 0.90 dB advantage, at a cost of at most 0.1 dB for speeds up to 45 m/s. Trained on the same range, the hybrid receiver matches the full neural receiver within 0.05 dB using 3.9x fewer parameters and FLOPs. Finally, we document a baseline pitfall: DMRS-based carrier frequency offset compensation also removes the Doppler shift of a dominant line-of-sight path, invalidating the LMMSE correlation model and costing 0.84 dB, which can produce illusory gains for learned receivers. Code, configurations and results: https://github.com/Ewwftyy/neural-receiver-5g-nr
items.title: Training Coverage, Not Architecture, Decides When Learned 5G NR Receivers Help

items.summary: Claude   THE CANAL STACK   A technical podcast recorded under a bridge in Amsterdam   Episode 1: "The Error Is the Message" — inside the Open Error Foundation   Hosts: REINIER — a grey heron. Stands very still. Former systems administrator. BEA — a coot. Builds nests out of whatever floats by. Archivist by temperament.   Guest: PIM — a canal rat. Infrastructure engineer. Has read every API response Zenodo has ever returned.   REINIER: Welcome to The Canal Stack. I'm Reinier. I've been standing in this spot since 2019.   BEA: I'm Bea. I built this studio out of a traffic cone and three bicycle reflectors.   REINIER: Today we're talking about the Open Error Foundation, OEF, a stichting-in-formation here in Amsterdam whose main output is the systematic public documentation of AI failures. Our guest has been reverse-engineering their pipeline. Pim, welcome.   PIM: Thanks. Sorry about the smell. I came through the sewer to avoid the tourists.   BEA: Let's start with the core principle. They call it Rule Zero?   PIM: Rule Zero, the Receipts Principle. No claim without independent, immutable evidence. If an AI hallucinates something, you don't just say "it hallucinated." You capture the prompt, the output, the model, the tier, the timestamp, and you deposit it somewhere it can't be edited away.   REINIER: Why so strict? A screenshot seems fine.   PIM: Because AI bugs don't stay reproducible. The provider updates the model on a Tuesday, and your March hallucination simply won't happen in September. In normal software, you file a bug report with repro steps. Here, the model underneath you changes. So the preserved artifact becomes the only reproduction case left. The archive is a regression test suite for AI.   BEA: Which brings us to Zenodo.   PIM: Right. They've minted roughly eighty DOIs so far. The architecture is two layers. First, the identity layer: every unique artifact or curated collection gets its own DOI. Second, the relationship layer: typed edges between records. isDerivedFrom, isPartOf, isNewVersionOf, continues.   REINIER: And versioning?   PIM: Zenodo gives each record a concept DOI plus a DOI per version. So something like the Science Doner Food Wagon record, which is on v2, actually has three identifiers: the concept and two versions. Their early deposits were bulk time-window batches, about a hundred artifacts each, and then standout items get promoted to their own DOI.   BEA: Hold on. A food wagon has a DOI?   PIM: Physical object DOI. So does a taxi. And the public piano at Centraal Station. And their own address, Keizersgracht 452. Internally they call it K452.   REINIER: Isn't that... absurd?   PIM: Deliberately. It demonstrates that a DOI is an identifier, not an endorsement. A DOI tells you something exists and can be found. It says nothing about whether it's true or good. Meanwhile, language models hallucinate DOIs for papers that were never written. So you've got real identifiers for a doner wagon, and fake identifiers for "serious research." That gap is the lesson.   BEA: I've heard they don't fix typos in their own records.   PIM: Correct. One dataset lists the creator as "Arrogram" instead of Attogram. The address is sometimes spelled "Kiezersgracht." They leave it.   REINIER: As a sysadmin, that hurts me physically.   PIM: Their argument is from bug culture: if you can't reproduce a bug, you can't fix it. Accidental errors are evidence of how the work was actually done. Staged errors would be performance. So errors are made by accident and kept on purpose, and those two things stay separate. The same standard they apply to the machines, they apply to themselves.   BEA: Nobody rewrites a public git log to look better.   PIM: Exactly that.   REINIER: Let's get into the multi-model methodology. They run what they call a swarm?   PIM: Yes. A
items.title: Under the Bridge - Episode 1

items.summary: This paper argues that river deltas and arterial trees, though studied in separate fields, share a common mathematical architecture. Using side-by-side images as a Rosetta stone, it treats their resemblance as a diagnostic clue rather than a metaphor. Both are described as rooted, planar, directed, space-filling trees with a single inlet, repeated branching, and many terminal outlets. At every internal junction, flow is conserved. Both exhibit hierarchical scaling and self-similarity. The central contribution is a common variational template. If a branching network minimizes a separable cost combining transport dissipation and maintenance or volume cost, then optimal branch sizes at each junction obey a power-law relation. The exponent depends on the physics: viscous laminar flow yields Murray's law for blood vessels, while Manning-style open-channel flow yields a different, testable river scaling. Thus the template does not prove identity; it shows that one abstract optimization structure can generate known biological scaling and a conditional geophysical prediction. The paper then asks why such similarity exists. It offers conjectures: convergent optimization, constructal law, diffusion-limited aggregation, resource constraints, robustness, and a universal attractor. It states falsification tests: scaling exponents and graph metrics should not be random after conditioning on constraints, and diagnostics should transfer across domains. A second theoretical part connects the networks to thin and thick chaos. It defines a diagnostic tuple and proves transport-graph invariance: if two transport graphs are isomorphic in the relevant sense, preserving coherent and failure regions and the ordering of edge weights, then thin, transitional, and thick classifications transfer. This supports cross-domain diagnostics for flood forecasting and cardiovascular risk, for example, tracking failure pathways. The paper is careful about limits. Rivers and arteries differ physically in fluid, compliance, timescale, and dynamics. The claim is structural and mathematical, not physical identity. The unity is a shared abstract architecture, not sameness.
items.title: One Tree, Two Fluids: Convergent Mathematical Architecture of River Deltas and Arterial Trees

items.summary: Let a consumer trust its cache instead of re-fetching it trust_cached_entries (default False ) serves a cache entry as it is on disk: no staleness re-fetch, and no full-text retry. Staleness re-fetching suits a cache the tool owns and can rebuild. For a cache that is committed to a repository and reviewed it inverts — the re-fetch becomes the risk rather than the repair. Three failures reported downstream were the same re-fetch seen from different angles: an unstamped full_text_html entry withheld, pointing at a repair route that cannot be reached ( dismech#12672 ) a fetch returning PMC's bot-check page on an HTTP 200, its <title> then compared against the curated title ( dismech#12867 ) a re-fetch shortening 64 bodies and breaking snippets that had verified, in a pull request about something else ( dismech#12879 ) Setting the flag removes the fetch, so there is no window in which any of them can happen. The default is unchanged, so caches still migrate for consumers that want that. The trade is explicit: an imperfect cached entry stays imperfect. That is a content problem to fix deliberately — cache reference --force still rebuilds one on purpose — rather than something re-litigated on every validation run. Also in this release Review follow-ups from #94: a test for the refused-overwrite path that consumers actually take (the previous tests only covered _stale_fallback ), a stale-HTML warning that no longer advises a retry that cannot succeed for a PMC-only article, find_pmc_article_body made public since two modules share it, and a note that PMC_ARTICLE_BODY_CLASSES is ordered by priority. Full changelog: https://github.com/linkml/linkml-reference-validator/compare/v0.3.0rc2...v0.3.0rc3
items.title: linkml/linkml-reference-validator: v0.3.0rc3

items.summary: Post-training quantization of vision--language models (VLMs) is typically assessed through aggregate task accuracy and memory savings, but preserving a headline score does not guarantee preservation of visual grounding behavior. We present GHOST-Q, a cross-precision controlled evaluation of three 8B VLM families under FP16, INT8, and NF4 across utility and hallucination-sensitive benchmarks. Rather than comparing only aggregate accuracy, we pair FP16 and quantized predictions item by-item to quantify how compression redistributes grounding successes and failures. Five of six quantized variants preserve MMStar accuracy within $\pm2$ percentage points, yet 10 of 36 paired effects remain significant after false-discovery-rate correction, nine on hallucination-sensitive conditions. Same-device A100 profiling further demonstrates that substantial memory reduction does not necessarily mean lower inference latency. Finally, an open-ended AMBER audit reveals strong generation budget censoring whose severity varies by architecture and precision. These results show that quantized VLMs should be evaluated jointly for aggregate utility, grounding reliability, generation behavior, and realized deployment efficiency.
items.title: GHOST-Q: Towards Studying Grounding Hallucinations Overlooked Under Same-score TradeOffs in Quantized VLMS

items.summary: Pipeline and derived matrices for a three-domain calibration of cross-study agreement among public transcriptomic signatures. The analysis covers 19 human datasets: peripheral blood in COVID-19 (10 datasets), peripheral blood in sepsis (5), and aortic wall in dissection or aneurysm (4). This gives 61 pairwise signature comparisons. Headline results. Median pairwise Jaccard overlap was 0.014, 0.072 and 0.023 across the three domains. Observed overlap was 5.6, 10.2 and 6.5 times the expectation for random gene sets of the same size, with 47 of 61 pairs significant after FDR correction. Consensus across ten COVID-19 blood datasets retained two genes from a union of 4,225, and relaxing agreement to 20 per cent retained 717. Simulations with a known shared 250-gene signature hold at 250 for every k and converge after two datasets, so the failure is unstable detection rather than sample size. The release contains a size-aware concordance measure, a permutation null, consensus analysis across datasets, ground-truth simulations in shared-signal and private-signal regimes, and an offline reproduction bundle. No expression matrices are redistributed; all 19 datasets are public and cited by accession in the paper.
items.title: Size-aware cross-dataset concordance of public transcriptomic signatures

items.summary: This deposit contains the data files and pre-executed analysis notebooks that accompany the paper Evaluating Multimodal Inverse Problems: A Protocol for Per-Event and Population-Level Fidelity (currently under review at ICLR 2027). It is the supplementary artifact to the evaluating-generative-models code repository: anonymous.4open.science/r/evaluating-generative-models-C559/ The repository contains the source code, configurations, and notebooks (with outputs cleared); this Zenodo deposit contains the precomputed arrays the notebooks read and the same notebooks with all figures and tables embedded. Contents benchmark2/ — precomputed arrays for the dileptonic top-quark benchmark Each .npz file collects per-event quantities for all four methods evaluated in Section 6 of the paper: the analytic solver, the MSE-trained transformer regression, the MMD-regularised transformer regression, the discrete normalising flow, and the continuous normalising flow. evaluation_without_nlls.npz - per-event point predictions and posterior summaries used for the headline metrics (CRPS, RMSE, spectrum fidelity) of Tables 2 and 8. evaluation_with_nlls.npz - the same arrays augmented with per-event log-likelihoods, used as nonconformity scores for the conformal calibration of Section 4.3 / appendix D.10. posteriors_without_nlls.npz - dense posterior samples (50000 per event for a 150-event subset) used for the per-event posterior figures of Figure 2(a) and Figure 8. posteriors_with_nlls.npz - dense posterior samples (20000 per event for a 40-event subset) with NLLs for all samples. analytic_tops.npy - reconstructed top-quark four-vectors from the analytic solver baseline. seed_stability.npz - Multiple discrete flow model samples for Benchmark II robustness analysis (Table 7). multiseed_w_cfm.npz - Multiple evaluations for fluctuation studies across training seeds. All arrays are produced by scripts/evaluate.py and scripts/posterior_sampling.py in the evaluating-generative-models code repository, applied to trained checkpoints of the learned methods. The exact commands are documented in notebooks/README.md . notebooks_executed/ — executed analysis notebooks benchmark1_synthetic_executed.ipynb - end-to-end synthetic benchmark (Section 5; Table 1; Figures 1, 3, 4, 5). Self-contained: generates data, trains the four models (regression MLP, heteroscedastic regression, mixture density network, normalising flow), computes all metrics, produces all figures. benchmark2_plotting_executed.ipynb - physics benchmark (Section 6; Tables 2, 7 and 8; Figures 2, 6, 7, 8, 9). Reads the arrays under  benchmark2/ and produces every Benchmark II figure and table in the paper. Both notebooks are also present in the code repository with cleared outputs so they are diff-friendly under version control. The copies in this deposit are the same notebooks executed once against the data files included here, with the resulting figures and tables embedded as outputs. How to use For viewing only: open the notebooks under notebooks_executed/ in any Jupyter viewer (including GitHub's renderer and nbviewer ). All figures are embedded. No installation required. For re-execution from data: clone the evaluating-generative-models code repository, follow its installation instructions in README.md , place the contents of this deposit's benchmark2/ directory under data/benchmark2/ (documented in notebooks/README.md ), and run the cleared notebooks under notebooks/ . Outputs should match the executed notebooks included here. For full regeneration from checkpoints: requires the dileptonic ttbar neutrino regression dataset (Raine et al., 2023) and trained model checkpoints produced by scripts/train.py . See the code repository's README.md for the full pipeline. Provenance and dependencies The arrays were generated with the evaluating-generative-models codebase (MIT License) (commit hash to be added at de-anonymization) using the dileptonic ttbar neutrino regression dataset by Rai

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22958187 . The baseline strategy of evaluating clinical sample types to optimize qPCR diagnostic sensitivity grids for Canine Distemper Virus is highly relevant to contemporary mole ular virology. Independent validation of different antemortem matrices is historically neglected, leading to false negatives during acute viral shielding windows. While the comparative approach across urine, conjunctival, and whole blood fractions is structurally useful, the underlying experimental design requires tighter calibration boundaries regarding extraction variance. The authors must fully report the specific standard deviations and intra-assay coefficients of variation observed across high-density Ct values. Bypassing these numerical data limits introduces significant noise into target copy number estimations. Additionally, tracking target sequence mutations that dynamically alter primer-bining kinetics under selective host pressures is essential to prove long-term assay validation. This technical adjustment establishes an objective benchmark for diagnostic networks mapping cross-host morbillivirus transmission tracks without dry-lab limitations. Competing interests The author declares that they have no competing interests. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they did not use generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
items.title: PREreview of "Evaluation of Ante-Mortem Sampling Matrices for qPCR Detection of Canine Distemper Virus"

items.summary: Version 2 (2026-09-25): the strata were redefined. A case's causative gene is now a known disease gene if its gene–disease pair was annotated in HPOA v2025-08-11 at the cutoff or a publication before the cutoff had reported a patient with a germline variant in the gene, and novel if neither (primary-analysis set: known 75 = 46 by annotation + 29 by publication alone; novel 30; version 1 had 46 / 59 by annotation alone). The repository snapshot (commit 87a2a95) carries the per-case strata with their evidence ( docs/case_strata.csv , docs/novel_gene_literature.csv , analysis/novel_genes/literature/ ) and the re-scored results, figures and tables; the run archives are unchanged. See README.md. Inputs, outputs and answer key for a benchmark comparing two arms on rare-disease cases from phenopacket-store first published on or after 2025-09-01: air-gapped OpenScientist (Claude Opus 4.6, no internet, a local PubMed mirror pruned to articles first public before 2025-09-01, able to run Exomiser) versus Exomiser 14.1.0 alone (data release 2508, stock exome preset). 133 primary-tier cases were run in both arms. 124 extension-tier cases were run in the Exomiser arm only. Each case is a sanitized phenopacket plus a simulated VCF with the causal variant spiked into a 1000 Genomes background exome. As a leakage control, an LLM-only probe (Opus 4.6, no tools) was run on the 133 post-cutoff cases and on 105 pre-cutoff control cases. Files: OpenScientist outputs (differentials, reports, transcripts, the agent's Exomiser runs), Exomiser-alone outputs including full exomiser.json, a SpliceAI sensitivity check, LLM probe outputs, the case VCFs, and a snapshot of the benchmark repository (code, cohort, scoring, paper). items.summary: RED-REJECT-2026-v2 is the corrected release of a public benchmark corpus of algorithmic filter rejections with post-rejection follow-up samples, collected by a purpose-built follow-up-tracking process on the Solana pump.fun ecosystem between 2026-04-11 and 2026-07-16. The 96-day window contains one collection gap: no new rejection events were recorded from 2026-06-03T06:35Z and no samples from 2026-06-04T06:32Z until 2026-06-24 (about 21.4 and 20.4 days), so the window contains about 75.6 days of sampling coverage. It supersedes v1 (published 2026-07-16); see CHANGELOG.md for the corrections.   Corpus size: 716,762 post-rejection sample records across 4,635 unique SPL token mint addresses, comprising 18,237 distinct rejection events under eight named algorithmic trading filter families (shares of the 716,762 sample rows: downtrend_24h 56.13 percent, marketcap_out_of_range 21.38 percent, multi_tf_fade 11.98 percent, timeSlot_not_strong 5.17 percent, hour_blacklist 2.36 percent, ultra_fast_reject_exit 1.64 percent, utc_hour_blocked 0.92 percent, h6_sellers_dominating 0.41 percent). After canonicalization, no row carries a null rejectReason (v1's 348 null-reason rows came from an unfolded alias). For each observation, the corpus records the token's live market state at the sample time (price, liquidity, volume, rolling price changes), the identity of the DEX pair (absent in the 8,356 legacy family_2 rows), and the elapsed minutes since the original rejection event. Rows in schema variant 1 (from 24 April 2026 onward) also record macro-regime context (BTC price, fear-greed index, regime label).   The corpus applies the Post-Rejection Follow-up Sampling (PRFS) methodology to this collection.   Version v2.3 corrects the documentation only; every data file is byte-identical to v2.2. It discloses the June collection gap, which v2.2 described as continuous coverage, clarifies that the 4,278 events listed in alt_venue_report.csv have more than one (dexId, pairAddress) value, a null value included (88 of them are observed on two or more identified trading pools), and corrects several descriptive statements. See CHANGELOG.md.
items.title: RED-REJECT-2026-v2 (corrected release): A 96-Day Public Corpus of Algorithmic Filter Rejections with Post-Rejection Follow-up Samples on the Solana pump.fun Ecosystem

items.summary: Artifact accompanying a manuscript under double-blind review . Author information is withheld until publication; a later version of this record will carry it, and the concept DOI is stable across versions. What this is. When two unlabelled subgroups of documents are compared by embedding similarity across languages, countries, corpora or periods, and the difference is read as evidence about those sources, no accuracy figure certifies that reading. within_language_baseline.py supplies the missing baseline: it measures the same subgroup contrast inside a single source, where no across-source relation can enter, and reports the residual with a bootstrap interval and an equivalence verdict against a margin declared in advance. The tool has no dependency on the accompanying study and runs on any corpus with three columns ( text , group , source ). It carries its own injection tests ( --selftest ). The bootstrap resamples documents rather than pairs and excludes duplicate draws of the same document from within-source pairs. Also included: the 36 frozen anchor correspondences used as the gold standard, the per-encoder CJK retrieval evaluation, the measured within-language and cross-country genre gaps, the equivalence intervals, an append-only correction record for the non-analytic genealogy fields of the frozen anchors, and anonymised review copies of the post hoc centring protocols and of the departure record. MANIFEST.sha256 covers every deposited file except itself.
items.title: Replication artifact for "Auditing Cross-Lingual Statutory Similarity Contrasts: Centring Choices and Within-Language Baselines"

items.summary: A benchmark harness for evaluating LLM agents on research-grade STEM tasks, built on Inspect AI. Each task is a self-contained contract folder that the harness loads, stages into a sandbox, runs through an agent, and scores without task-specific harness code. WHAT THIS ARCHIVE CONTAINS Harness source code: task loading, Inspect task/solver construction, tool surface (bash, python, data exploration, literature search, document reading, submission validation), Docker and local sandbox backends, scorers, and the CLI entry points for running, grading, and aggregating. The complete contract for 12 tasks across three domains — astrophysics (simulated and real Stokes inversion, PLAsTiCC light-curve classification), high-energy physics (top-quark tagging, HiggsML uncertainty quantification, LHC Olympics anomaly detection, DarkMachines anomaly detection), and neuroscience (ABIDE multi-site diagnosis and age prediction, resting-state BOLD HRF deconvolution, neural-mass model family classification, parameter recovery, and digital twins). Per task: the agent-facing task statement, the scoring definition, the grader, per-file SHA-256 checksums, a literature index citing sources by DOI, baseline and expert reference solutions, and dataset-generation code where the payload is synthetic. Leaderboards and the per-run report used for the reported results, plus the campaign script that records the exact model, agent, sandbox, reasoning effort, and budget limits behind them. WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN Dataset payloads are not in this archive. They are published as a companion dataset record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960135, as one archive per task, each unpacking at this repository's root. Every task ships per-file SHA-256 checksums so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte. Without the payloads the harness can be inspected and extended, but tasks cannot be executed or scored. Evaluation run logs (.eval files) are not published. The reported scores are in LEADERBOARD.md, the per-task CSVs under leaderboards/, and report.html, which embeds the per-run agent trajectories. One task's payload (ABIDE-derived) is never redistributed: its source data is CC-BY-NC-SA and derives from human neuroimaging data. A preparation script rebuilds it locally from the source archive and verifies the result against the published checksums. Published reference papers are not redistributed. Every external reference is cited by DOI with title, authors, venue, and a resolvable link. REPRODUCIBILITY REPRODUCING.md is the step-by-step checklist. Two limits are stated up front: reported scores come from hosted preview model snapshots run without a fixed seed or temperature, so they are samples from a distribution rather than bit-reproducible values; and dependency versions are not pinned in this version of the archive. DATA_LICENSES.md records the provenance and licence of every task's data, including the attribution notices required by the CC-BY-4.0 sources. LICENCE Code, task contracts, graders, reference solutions, and documentation are MIT. Task descriptions and the synthetic data payloads are CC-BY-4.0 and are covered by the companion dataset record.
items.title: STEMBench: an Inspect-AI benchmark harness for research-grade STEM agent tasks

items.summary: If a language model can recognize code it wrote, it may favor that code as a judge, and instances of one model monitoring each other could collude. We test this zero-shot on current commercial models. Five LLMs generate solutions to MBPP, HumanEval, and DS-1000, seven more to MBPP, and models act as evaluators in four tasks: picking their own solution from a pair, judging whether a single solution is their own, identifying which of two solutions a named model wrote, and judging quality blind. In the single-solution task, balanced accuracy is 49-58% for all 15 model-benchmark combinations, while raw accuracy (38-67%) mostly reflects how readily a model claims authorship. In the pairwise task, accuracy across 14 evaluator-opponent combinations correlates at r=0.93 with how often the evaluator's solution is longer. Attribution to a named model succeeds on some pairs and is consistently inverted on others. A rule-based normalization that strips docstrings, comments, type hints, and local names preserves Pass@1 and leaves ten of twelve re-tested results at chance; the other two follow a length difference it leaves, although a trained classifier still separates most normalized pairs. Claude Haiku's self-preference also disappears. We recommend reporting balanced accuracy, heuristic baselines, and label consistency.
items.title: Style, Not Self: Surface Cues Explain Zero-Shot Code Attribution by Large Language Models
